query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, frictional sliding on a multi-phase eutectic HEA induces a protective oxide film that initially lowers wear but eventually undergoes cyclic stress-induced spallation, exposing reactive phases and thereby accelerating both wear and localized corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a lamellar microstructure composed of FCC and B2 (or BCC/B2) phases.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to reciprocating sliding wear in a corrosive (chloride-containing) environment at elevated temperatures (e.g., ~800 °C) with standard loading cycles.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (>750 °C), atmospheric exposure with chloride ions present, and cyclic mechanical shear (reciprocating wear test).
generation.structural_mediator: A transient, friction-induced oxide film primarily comprising Fe-oxides and other oxide components that eventually spalls off, exposing the underlying eutectic phases.
generation.mechanism: Friction at high temperature results in oxide film formation that initially reduces friction, but repeated cyclic stresses induce mechanical fatigue and spallation of the oxide. The exposed reactive phases (including hard, brittle intermetallic or σ phases) become susceptible to further mechanical removal and microgalvanic corrosion, thus accelerating the overall material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Total degradation (material loss) increases by an approximated 2-3× factor relative to a baseline exhibiting a stabilized oxide layer. Individually, wear depth increases (due to adhesive wear from spallation) and localized corrosion (pitting density) is enhanced relative to a condition with a more robust oxide film.
generation.baseline: Comparison with a control sample where the oxide film is artificially stabilized (e.g., via surface treatment or alloying modification) under identical wear and corrosion test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism holds when the testing temperature is sufficiently high to thermally activate rapid oxidation and when the mechanical loading frequency is high enough to generate cyclic shear stresses; in environments lacking aggressive ions, the corrosion component may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of oxide spallation versus inherent abrasive wear may vary with microstructural heterogeneity and oxide composition; additionally, long-term cyclic behavior may introduce factors not captured in short-duration tests.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples, one with standard processing and the other with an added pre-oxidation or surface modification treatment aimed at enhancing oxide film stability. Subject both sets to identical reciprocating wear tests in a chloride-rich environment at 800 °C.
measurements: Measure wear depth and friction coefficient evolution over time.
Assess the extent of oxide film presence via SEM/XRD after testing.
Perform localized corrosion mapping to quantify pitting density.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples (with stabilized oxide film) do not exhibit significantly lower wear rates and localized corrosion compared to the untreated samples, or if spallation and subsequent degradation rates do not differ, then the hypothesis that oxide film spallation governs accelerated degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.

This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance. papers.title: Influence of Laser Power on CoCrFeNiMo High-Entropy Alloy Coating Microstructure and Properties.
papers.approach: Laser cladding under variable laser power (2000 W, 2250 W, 2500 W) with microstructural analysis (SEM) and wear testing.
papers.findings: A complex tri‐phase microstructure (gray, white, black phases) evolves with laser power. At lower power, hypereutectic structures dominate and progressively transition toward a fully eutectic structure. During wear, frictional heating promotes the formation of an oxide layer that eventually undergoes stress accumulation, leading to adhesive wear and spallation of hard σ-phase particles.
papers.mechanism: Friction-induced oxidation forms a protective oxide that later experiences stress‐induced spallation; this oxide breakdown exposes underlying phases, accelerating material loss under coupled wear–corrosion conditions.

papers.title: High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy fabricated by spark plasma sintering
papers.approach: Reciprocating wear tests from room temperature up to 900 °C combined with XRD and SEM analysis of wear tracks.
papers.findings: Wear resistance is slightly reduced up to intermediate temperatures and then improved at very high temperatures (800–900 °C). The wear tracks reveal formation of protective oxide films (e.g., a spinel phase) that diminish wear depth, though the oxide layer may be mechanically fragile.
papers.mechanism: Elevated temperatures enable the formation of a protective, yet sometimes unstable, oxide film that modifies friction and wear behavior; the film’s mechanical instability can contribute to accelerated degradation when it spalls off.

papers.title: Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation.
papers.system: Ni-based complex concentrated alloy with a nanohierarchical architecture
papers.approach: Design and testing of nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates under sliding conditions at various temperatures; analysis including nanoindentation and cross-sectional SEM.
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits an ultralow wear rate (10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁶ mm³/Nm) from room temperature to 800 °C. At high temperatures, a dense glaze layer forms, providing robust friction protection. Nanostructural features distribute deformation and build up adaptive friction interface protection.
papers.mechanism: A self-adaptive friction interface protection mechanism arises from cooperative deformation of nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates, which gradually release frictional stress and inhibit spallation of the protective oxide/glaze layer.

papers.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coatings on Q235 steel with varying boron content
papers.approach: Laser cladding with controlled boron microalloying; comprehensive tribological tests and electrochemical corrosion measurements.
papers.findings: Boron addition preserves the BCC and σ phases while promoting in situ formation of TiB₂ particles, refining the microstructure and improving microhardness. Lower B content enhances passive film stability leading to better corrosion resistance, whereas excessive B leads to defects accelerating degradation.
papers.mechanism: Boron microalloying modifies the lattice through TiB₂ precipitation, which influences the passive film formation and mechanical integrity of the coating. This refinement helps mitigate coupled degradation under simultaneous wear–corrosion but overshoots can trigger localized film failure.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperature
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (dual-phase: L12 FCC and B2 BCC) in chloride-containing sulfuric acid
papers.approach: Electrochemical measurements, XPS, EBSD, and SEM analysis to correlate microstructure (phase distribution and elemental segregation) with corrosion modes at various temperatures.
papers.findings: At lower temperatures, stable passive films form on Al-Ni-rich phases leading to limited localized corrosion. At elevated temperatures, the passive film becomes unstable, and galvanic coupling between dissimilar phases (e.g., L12 vs. B2) induces more severe pitting and selective dissolution.
papers.mechanism: Microgalvanic coupling between phases with distinct corrosion potentials—combined with temperature-induced passive film instability—results in accelerated, localized corrosion, which under mechanically active wear conditions can synergistically enhance degradation.

papers.title: Effect of Post-Heat Treatment on Microstructure and Corrosion Property of Additively Manufactured AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-E.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy fabricated by laser melting deposition
papers.approach: Post-heat treatment at temperatures from 600 °C to 1000 °C with subsequent microstructural and corrosion testing (potentiodynamic and immersion tests).
papers.findings: Increased heat-treatment temperature enlarges interlamellar spacing and FCC phase fraction, improving uniform corrosion resistance up to a point; however, treatments above 800 °C promote Al enrichment in the BCC phase, leading to enhanced pitting corrosion due to compromised passive film integrity.
papers.mechanism: Temperature-modulated phase evolution alters the balance between FCC and BCC phases, influencing the distribution of reactive elements (e.g., Al) and thus affecting galvanic interactions and passive film stability; this in turn modulates corrosion behavior under combined wear exposure.

established: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (HEAs) typically exhibit dual-phase microstructures (e.g., FCC + BCC/B2 or lamellar eutectic arrangements) that critically influence wear and corrosion responses.
Elevated temperatures promote friction-induced oxidation; the resulting oxide films can initially provide protection but may eventually spall off under cyclic mechanical stresses.
Galvanic coupling between chemically or structurally distinct phases can exacerbate localized corrosion, particularly when passive films are compromised.
Nanohierarchical or refined microstructures can adaptively manage frictional stresses, indicating that controlled microstructural design can influence degradation behavior.

approaches_tried.approach: Laser cladding with variable energy input
approaches_tried.outcome: Manipulated phase composition and microstructure to control oxidative wear and corrosion; low power led to heterogeneous microstructures prone to oxide spallation.
Produced dense, multi-phase HEAs with high hardness and improved wear resistance at elevated temperatures due to protective oxide formation.
Refined phase size through TiB₂ formation, enhancing passive film integrity and wear resistance at optimal boron levels while excessive B led to defects.

approaches_tried.approach: Post-heat treatment of additively manufactured eutectic HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Altered phase fractions to improve uniform corrosion resistance, though higher treatment temperatures increased pitting due to galvanic effects.

mechanisms: Friction-induced oxidation generating a protective oxide layer that later spalls due to cyclic shear stresses.
Microgalvanic coupling between dissimilar phases (e.g., FCC vs. BCC/B2 or L12 vs. B2) that accelerates localized pitting corrosion.
Adaptive friction interface protection via cooperative deformation in nanohierarchical architectures that can delay wear by forming a dense glaze layer.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize the protective role of high-temperature oxide films in reducing wear, while others report that these films become mechanically unstable and accelerate degradation.

There is variation in attributing improvements in wear resistance either to a self-adaptive, nanostructure-driven mechanism or to conventional oxide-layer formation, indicating a conflict in the dominant mechanistic interpretation.
open_questions: How do the mechanically induced spallation of oxide films and the ensuing exposure of reactive phases quantitatively contribute to the accelerated degradation in eutectic HEAs exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion?
What is the relative impact of microgalvanic coupling versus mechanical wear in the overall degradation rate under elevated temperature conditions?
How can controlled modifications (e.g., microalloying or post-processing) be optimized to improve the stability of passive films under synergistic degradation conditions?
opportunities: Design controlled comparative experiments between eutectic HEAs with homogenized microstructures and those with intentionally heterogeneous phase distributions to isolate the effects of galvanic coupling versus oxide film spallation.
Investigate the role of alloying additions (e.g., boron) and tailored heat treatments in stabilizing oxide layers and reducing microgalvanic corrosion under combined wear–corrosion conditions.

Explore in situ monitoring of oxide film integrity and phase-specific degradation during simultaneous mechanical and chemical attack to establish clear falsification criteria for the proposed mechanistic hypothesis.

directions.direction: Friction‐induced oxide film formation and subsequent spallation exposes reactive internal phases.
directions.assessment: Directly relates to the coupled wear–corrosion acceleration by linking mechanical shear (wear) with the breakdown of a transient oxide barrier. Well supported by observations of friction‐induced oxide formation and its later spallation (e.g. PMC12156342::web::036::3_2_mechanical_properties, PMC12156342::web::042::4_conclusions). Feasible by comparing oxide‐stabilized versus untreated coatings.

directions.direction: Enhanced microgalvanic coupling between dissimilar phases under high temperature due to passive film instability.
directions.assessment: Addresses the corrosion part of the degradation, as the unstable passive films on different phases (e.g. FCC vs. B2/BCC) lead to galvanic attacks amplified by wear exposing fresh interfaces. Evidence is available (PMC9319277::web::022::3_4_corrosion_observation, PMC12735082::web::019::4_conclusions).

directions.direction: Thermally induced mismatch and interfacial cracking in the eutectic lamellae accelerating degradation under cyclic wear.
directions.assessment: Attacks the limitation by hypothesizing that differential thermal expansion between phases creates mechanical cracks that both weaken the structure and allow accelerated corrosion at those defect sites. Supported indirectly by studies on post-heat treatment and phase evolution (PMC12735082::web::000::abstract).

directions.direction: Failure of the adaptive friction interface protection in nanohierarchical eutectic structures at elevated temperatures.
directions.assessment: Proposes that the self-adaptive, nanostructure-mediated friction protection breaks down under cyclic high-temperature load, leading to spallation and increased degradation. This approach leverages findings on nano-coupled grain behavior (PMC10241162::web::015::remarkable_wear_resistance_and_wear_mech) and is testable using microstructural tuning.
